2611.06770.title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management
2611.06770.abstract: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

2611.06353.title: Traffic-VL: Reinforced Vision-Language Models for Generalizable End-to-End Traffic Signal Control
2611.06353.abstract: Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.

2611.06204.title: CoSafe: Cooperative Runtime Safety Assurance for Mixed-Traffic Autonomous Driving
2611.06204.abstract: With the rapid development of autonomous driving systems (ADSes), real-world roads are evolving into mixed-traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and other traffic participants (e.g., human-driven vehicles (HDVs), cyclists, and pedestrians) coexist and interact with each other. However, current ADSes still incur various safety violations in mixed traffic scenarios, raising a strong demand for runtime safety assurance frameworks that can continuously monitor hazards and prevent potential violations. Existing ego-centric assurance approaches are insufficient for mixed traffic, where violations often arise from locally reasonable yet jointly incompatible decisions among multiple vehicles and cannot be reliably resolved through independent takeover. To bridge this gap, we propose CoSafe, a modular and ADS-agnostic cooperative runtime safety assurance framework for mixed-traffic autonomous driving to extend runtime safety assurance from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention. CoSafe leverages vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to enable roadside units (RSUs) to monitor scene-level hazards and jointly mitigate hazards involving multiple vehicles. We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes, and our evaluation on the InterDrive benchmark demonstrates that CoSafe improves the driving score of AVs by 70.03% on average, reduces safety violations by 87.80%, and accurately identifies unsafe AVs with an F3 score of 0.930, while satisfying real-time constraints.

2611.06162.title: A Layered View of LLM Support in Underwater Robotics
2611.06162.abstract: This extended abstract discusses a specific and, in our experience, practically relevant role for large language models (LLMs) in underwater robotics. Our main premise is that, in underwater fielding missions, the immediate difficulty is often not the synthesis of new low-level control laws, but the operation of complex robotic systems under limited communications, partial observability, and expensive field time. In particular, a significant fraction of the effort during sea trials is devoted to fault diagnosis, telemetry interpretation, mission adjustment, and coordination across heterogeneous assets and operators. We argue that LLMs may be useful at this higher operational level, especially when grounded in structured vehicle state, alarms, logs, mission context, and existing planning or validation tools. At the same time, current limitations in grounding, consistency, and causal reasoning make these systems lack the predictability required to guarantee direct control, especially in real-world critical applications, although we do not exclude a future evolution in this direction. This viewpoint suggests a layered architecture in which conventional autonomy remains responsible for control, perception, estimation, and validated mission execution, whereas LLM-based modules serve as an additional support layer for debugging, operator interaction, constrained replanning support, orchestration, and post-mission analysis.

2611.06007.title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
2611.06007.abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.

2611.05448.title: Jev with Foresight: Safe Language-Guided Autonomous Driving via a Language World Model
2611.05448.abstract: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.

2611.05249.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
2611.05249.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.

2611.04710.title: DenseTwins: Dense Modality Decoupling for Multimodal Self-Supervision
2611.04710.abstract: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/DenseTwins.

2611.04034.title: Do Pretrained Backbones Transfer to Physical Sensors? A Systematic Study of Multimodal Initialization Across the Sensor Stack
2611.04034.abstract: Transfer learning from pretrained backbones has become standard practice in multi-sensor computer vision---yet two questions remain open: which pretrained weights transfer best to multi-sensor setups, and can in-domain pretraining outperform off-the-shelf solutions? Frameworks like MultiMAE demonstrate the utility of masked autoencoding in a multi-modal context, but rely entirely on dense, model-derived modalities. It is unclear how robustly these methods translate to real-world applications that use physical sensors, where the aggregation of diverse public datasets for large-scale pretraining inherently introduces modality sparsity. To investigate this systematically, we curate a multi-sensor autonomous driving collection of $2.82M$ images from 16 publicly available datasets, incorporating both physical hardware modalities (RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event) and model-derived modalities (Stereo Depth, Segmentation). We use this collection for in-domain pretraining based on the MultiMAE approach. We adapt MultiMAE's loss formulation to accommodate sparse samples, and study the effect of an enforced encoder bottleneck for modality alignment and of additional losses specific to dense reconstruction (SSIM and FFT). We then systematically compare against common pretrained backbones (ViT, MAE, DINO and MultiMAE) across downstream sensor fusion tasks. We find that MultiMAE is a surprisingly strong out-of-the-box baseline, transferring effectively even to modalities it has never seen, while our targeted modifications yield incremental but consistent improvements on multi-sensor transfer and overall robustness.

2611.04029.title: A Review of Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control Algorithms: State of the Art and Research Opportunities
2611.04029.abstract: Max-Pressure (MP) has emerged as a widely studied decentralized traffic signal control framework, thanks to its desirable theoretical properties and strong control performance. Early research on MP focused on improving control performance by exploring different variables of the traffic state for the definition of pressure. Subsequent studies expanded MP to incorporate the complexity of real-world transportation systems and emerging technologies. This paper provides a comprehensive review of these developments. The review first introduces the theoretical foundations of MP and examines early developments in movement weight definition. It then synthesizes major extensions for multimodal and multiscale network control, followed by recent developments in connected and automated vehicle (CAV) environments and the integration of MP with artificial intelligence (AI) and data-driven methods. Beyond summarizing existing approaches, this review examines their underlying assumptions, data requirements, implementation considerations, and practical limitations. Based on this comprehensive review, key research gaps and future directions are identified, including remaining limitations in the theoretical foundations of MP and the underexplored integration of autonomous vehicle control with the MP framework. Overall, this review provides a structured perspective on the evolution and current state of MP control and highlights opportunities for developing more proactive, robust, and practically deployable MP-based traffic control methods.

2611.02790.title: MultiMental-IAS: A Multimodal Driver Mental State Analysis Dataset for Context-Aware Non-IID Evaluation
2611.02790.abstract: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.

2611.02648.title: ReinSeg: Retrieval-Guided Bounded Multimodal Refinement for 3-D Road Anomaly Segmentation
2611.02648.abstract: 3-D road anomaly segmentation is essential for risk-aware perception in autonomous driving. Its central challenge is to rank sparsely observed hazards ahead of abundant normal road structures while preserving point-wise metric localization. LiDAR provides accurate 3-D point support, whereas surround-view imagery offers complementary semantic context for separating unexpected hazards from challenging normal structures. We propose ReinSeg, a retrieval-guided bounded multimodal refinement framework for point-wise road anomaly segmentation. Occupied LiDAR bird's-eye-view cells retrieve scene-specific context from a shared memory of eight surround-view images without supplying calibration variables to the retrieval module. A relative-norm-bounded residual returns this context to the LiDAR point features, so the frozen LIDO anomaly-scoring interface is preserved, and the refinement is optimized with in-distribution semantic labels only. On the Spotting the Unexpected (STU) benchmark, ReinSeg improves validation average precision from 27.54\% to 35.67\% and reduces the false-positive rate at 95\% anomaly recall from 34.85\% to 10.61\%, shrinking the high-recall screening set from 67.54 to 20.55 million points. Relative to REL, AP is 24.99 percentage points higher and FPR95 is 0.99 points lower. Matched interfaces and component isolation show that retrieved scene imagery and the relative-norm bound are both essential, and ReinSeg stays above LiDAR-only performance under missing, corrupted, or misaligned camera inputs while running at 21.8 frames per second. These results establish bounded retrieval of scene-specific visual evidence as an effective route to reliable 3-D road-hazard perception.

2611.02240.title: When to Probe and When to Act: Clarity-Aware Risk-Adaptive Control for Interactive Driving
2611.02240.abstract: Safe navigation in interactive traffic requires autonomous vehicles to reason about unobservable human characteristics and the reciprocal nature of multi-agent interactions. Traditional architectures often decouple prediction from planning, leading to the "Frozen Robot Problem" or unsafe maneuvers under high ambiguity because they treat risk assessment and information acquisition as independent objectives. We argue that the notion of safety should not remain static but must instead dynamically co-evolve with the system's internal confidence: the robot should actively clarify ambiguity when necessary while also recognizing the diminishing returns of information, and naturally transition toward task execution. We introduce a unified belief-space Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that couples multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) barrier mechanism. By treating clarity, a scalar informational state, as an explicit planning variable, the controller co-designs its probing strategy with its safety specification, tightening conservatism under high ambiguity and relaxing constraints as confidence improves. We further provide a performance analysis showing that the cost of information seeking and the expected planning-cost gap to a controller that knows the true human characteristic are bounded by residual ambiguity and solver error. We evaluate the framework in lane-merging and unsignalized-intersection scenarios against representative interactive-planning baselines. Across 5,000 simulations, the proposed method achieves the highest success rates (94.6% and 93.2%) and the lowest collision rates (1.2% and 1.4%) among the compared methods, providing a principled foundation for robust decision-making in human-centric environments.

2611.02157.title: Wireless Networks That See: Integrated Sensing and Communication in Complex Environments
2611.02157.abstract: The same radio interactions that complicate wireless communication can reveal what is happening around a network. Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) turns these interactions into opportunities to observe unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), road vehicles, and industrial mobile robots. Yet a strong echo is not necessarily a reliable object observation: stationary background can conceal motion, reflections can create virtual objects, and one viewpoint can leave part of an object's motion unobserved. This tutorial explains how known cellular signals are used to estimate propagation, suppress stationary background, interpret reflected paths, and combine observations from different sites. UAV examples under a Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) stochastic channel model and ray tracing in a San Francisco urban scene illustrate the mechanisms through spatial layouts, channel profiles, and before/after range--Doppler maps. Local checks reduce false outputs, with some loss of detection. Cooperation improves position accuracy for UAVs detected by both a single site and cooperating sites. The examples show how signal resources, measurement reporting, and application needs shape sensing performance, providing practical guidance for sensing services in complex environments.

2611.02076.title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
2611.02076.abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD

2611.01996.title: Safety4DM: A Vision-Language Framework for Risk-Aware Dynamic Maps in Vehicle-Road-Cloud Collaborative Driving
2611.01996.abstract: Dynamic map (DM) is a core information infrastructure for vehicle-road-cloud (VRC) cooperative autonomous driving. It fuses perception data from multiple sources to overcome the inherent line-of-sight and field-of-view limits of single-vehicle perception. However, DM still falls short on driving safety in two ways. First, DM data specifications already define road conditions semantically, but no pipeline yet turns real-world road observations into fine-grained risk entities in the DM. Second, existing DM systems lack a natural language interface for driving risks. To close these gaps, we propose Safety4DM, a safety-oriented language system for VRC dynamic maps. We first build RoadRisk, a real-world road image dataset that covers four types of road conditions and four risk levels. On this dataset, we fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) for road safety risk perception. The model outputs structured risk representations that the DM can ingest directly. We then introduce a Safety-aware Step-wise Prompting (SafeStep) mechanism as the natural language query interface of the DM. SafeStep answers queries accurately and also generates actionable driving advice. To build and evaluate this interface, we develop SafeVRC-Sim, a VRC cooperative simulation framework, and SafeDM-QA, a safety question-answering benchmark. Experiments show that even the compact Qwen3-VL-4B reaches 89.83% accuracy on risk perception after fine-tuning. SafeStep also plugs easily into multiple LLM families. With medium and large models (20B and above) from five families, it achieves over 93% natural language query accuracy in every case, which shows strong generalization.

2611.01286.title: An analytical model to explain under which conditions home batteries create new load peaks in the local grid
2611.01286.abstract: Simulation studies find that price-responsive home batteries and electric vehicles create new load peaks in low-voltage grids; with endogenous wholesale prices most of these peaks disappear. This paper explains both findings with an analytical model of the coincident peak at the transformer. The model is algebraic and solved in closed form, so the parameters that determine whether a new peak emerges and how large it becomes can be identified; they are few. The peak is the background load in the critical hour plus the charging of the local fleet. Under exogenous prices the charging equals the rated power of the fleet. Under endogenous prices the national fleet fills the trough of residual load until the price is flat; the depth of the fill follows from an energy balance in which the price function does not appear. For a V-shaped trough the local charging peak is the share of the grid in national flexibility times the square root of flank gradient times national flexibility. Rated power, price level, network charge and market size do not enter. The model reproduces simulated peaks for a German case within a few percent.

2611.00718.title: STEER: Route-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
2611.00718.abstract: Vision-language action (VLA) models excel for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet their tendency to over-invoke chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning mirrors a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as deliberate reasoning can slow or mislead human judgment in routine tasks, excessive CoT in VLA incurs unnecessary compute overhead and can paradoxically degrade planning performance. Recent research tackles this via adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity by selectively triggering CoT for complex scenes while responding directly to routine ones. While prior adaptive methods rely on implicit adaptation, recent work shows that explicitly optimizing the route between CoT and direct responses yields superior performance, assuming scene-difficulty annotations which are labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity. We explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved without any scene-difficulty labeling. We introduce STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring two key components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 demonstrate that STEER is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in both planning quality and the Pareto front of inference efficiency.

2610.42121.title: Where ADS Crashes Differ: A Harmonized Comparison Against Human Baselines
2610.42121.abstract: Crash-rate comparisons between automated driving systems (ADS) and human drivers require an exposure denominator that only a few operators publish. We instead ask a composition question: given a crash, does the mix of crash types differ between ADS and human-driven vehicles? The question needs no mileage and can therefore cover every ADS operator. We assemble the NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO) ADS incident files across both file generations into 2,450 distinct in-scope incidents (2021-2026), of which 828 fall within the 2021-2024 window covered by the Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), the national police-reported human comparator. A schema-constrained large language model (LLM) codes each SGO narrative into the CRSS crash-type taxonomy. Because SGO compels reporting far below the police-reporting threshold, we bracket reportability with an objective severity floor and a reasonable-person rubric, and claim a difference only where it survives both. Two composition differences hold under every reportability definition, tow definition and weighting of the human side, and under both definitions of driverless operation: turn-across-path crashes are under-represented among ADS crashes (0.23-0.46x the CRSS share under the primary driverless definition) and so are single-vehicle crashes (0.19-0.56x). In severity-floor rear-end crashes the ADS vehicle is the striking party at a quasi-induced-exposure ratio of 0.121 (95% CI [0.05, 0.23]) against a human baseline of 1.000. If the ADS vehicle is also struck more often than its exposure implies, this ratio overstates the ADS-human difference. We also document three pitfalls in the federal data: an operator-specific coding of driverless operation, a tow-away criterion confounded by fleet recovery practice, and an occupancy confound that accounts for about 42% of the apparent ADS-human severity gap.

2610.41352.title: CalibSwitch: Observation-Driven Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Recovery and Selective Maintenance for Multimodal Perception
2610.41352.abstract: Camera--LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image--point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884$^\circ$. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70\% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry--observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.

2610.40801.title: Drone-PUR: From Visual Clue Discovery to Understanding and Reasoning in UAV Scenes
2610.40801.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.

2610.40455.title: A Unified Benchmark for Aerial-Enhanced Autonomous Driving: The KITScenes Aerial Dataset
2610.40455.abstract: Aerial imagery provides complementary spatial context for autonomous driving by exposing road structure beyond the immediate perception range of onboard sensors. Yet map construction from aerial imagery, aerial-assisted online HD mapping, and cross-view localization are typically studied on separate data and benchmarks. We introduce KITScenes Aerial, an extension of the KITScenes Multimodal dataset that augments synchronized onboard sensor data, vehicle poses, and rich Lanelet2 map annotations with spatially associated aerial imagery and higher-resolution neural representations, providing a common basis for a variety of research tasks. Our mapping evaluation focuses on all 53 KITScenes map classes across different model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions, while retaining compatibility with the widely used three-class setting. Representative baselines show that aerial context is particularly beneficial for fine-grained and extended-range mapping, more than doubling 53-class mAP at the larger mapping extent. Higher-resolution aerial imagery yields a further 4.3 mAP (+24 %) improvement, with gains extending to challenging map elements such as traffic lights. We additionally evaluate cross-view localization under geographically disjoint conditions, where an adapted fine-grained feature-matching baseline achieves a mean translation error of 5.13 m. KITScenes Aerial thus enables unified study of aerial and ground-level information across complementary mapping and localization tasks. Project page: https://kitscenes.com/aerial

2611.08449.title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
2611.08449.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

2611.08441.title: Edge-Assisted Crowdsensing for Explainable Cyclist Safety Perception
2611.08441.abstract: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

2611.08436.title: SM4RT: Cascaded Feed-forward Model for 4D Reconstruction
2611.08436.abstract: We introduce SM4RT, a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction from RGB videos. While existing feed-forward approaches typically address geometry reconstruction and motion estimation separately--and often predict motions in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement--SM4RT solves these tasks sequentially by first reconstructing 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion estimation from the predicted structure. By expressing each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame, SM4RT reduces ambiguity arising from camera motion. To address the sparsity of real-world motion labels, SM4RT further incorporates a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step. We evaluate motion estimation on three dynamic-scene datasets--Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey--and SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines. We additionally benchmark geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets and show that SM4RT achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our unified framework demonstrates that combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade not only avoids performance trade-offs but also enhances motion estimation through improved geometric reasoning.

2611.08070.title: Can an LLM Actually Reason and Program about Neural Network's Weights or is it just memorization on steroids? Exploring "Weight-Space Programming"
2611.08070.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of neural networks directly, a capability termed weight-space programming. We ask whether the reading side of this capability reflects reasoning about weight flows or a combination of local arithmetic at the network's edges and memorized priors over public datasets. We test Claude Opus 5.5 on small convolutional networks of about 125,000 parameters trained on five image datasets, providing every weight as plain text with no tools, no forward passes, and no dataset or class names. The model performs accurate local calculations: batch-normalization statistics lead it to infer about three optimizer steps on networks stopped after three updates, and output-layer sign patterns recover the vehicle/animal split of CIFAR-10. The sessions report reading the first and last layers closely and sampling the middle, and several claims built on partial tracing fail verification, although we did not run a direct forward-pass test. Semantic judgments lean on familiar datasets: the model names CIFAR-10 for CIFAR-10 networks but also for all three fast-food networks, relabels KMNIST as MNIST, reads a 99.57%-accurate SAT-6 network as CIFAR-10 animal photos, and calls "frog" the output favored by a feature that fires most on trees. Permuting CIFAR-10's labels preserves the output split at the new indices, but every class pair the model interprets is then wrong, indicating reliance on remembered label order. These are exploratory results from mostly single runs. We conclude that zero-shot weight reading by this model is better described as local arithmetic plus dataset priors than as weight-flow tracing, and we provide a protocol for auditing future weight-space claims.

2611.07540.title: Action-Conditioned VLM Monitoring for Autonomous Vehicle Semantic Anomalies
2611.07540.abstract: We study action-conditioned monitoring of autonomous-vehicle behavior in semantically unusual driving scenes. The target is whether the executed ego action is appropriate for the scene: the same scene can admit both normal and anomalous behavior, so visual unusualness alone does not determine the monitoring label. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) first predicts the scene-required action from an outcome-hidden video window; the monitor then compares that expectation with the realized ego-motion trajectory under an explicit compatibility rule. To study this monitoring task, we contribute a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios spanning both failure polarities (42 derived from documented incidents), a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories, and an exploratory two-stage monitor on that corpus. On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, the two-stage protocol with a fixed T-2.5 s window obtains 83.0% accuracy and anomaly recall 0.773, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage video-only baseline; specificity is 0.880 versus 0.928.

2611.07537.title: Unified Overview of Safety Certificate Functions: Techniques from Hamilton--Jacobi Reachability and Control Barrier Functions
2611.07537.abstract: Safety is a central concern in modern autonomous systems. Safety certificates---functions whose existence guarantees that a system meets its safety specification---have long been used as a principled tool for rigorously reasoning about safety. Methods for synthesizing such certificates are scattered across research areas, with little guidance on when to use a particular approach. This tutorial provides a holistic treatment of safety certificate synthesis centered on two widely used families: Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis and control barrier functions (CBFs). For each family of methods, we first introduce its general formulation, along with classical and learning-based tools for certificate synthesis. Next, we introduce two benchmark problems consisting of vehicle systems of differing complexity to assess the certificate quality of different synthesis methods and their effectiveness in safety-critical control. We use these benchmarks to compare various methods and provide practical guidance for selecting an approach.

2611.07122.title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
2611.07122.abstract: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

2611.07081.title: Wide View Synthesis from Overlapping Perspective Cameras in Autonomous Driving
2611.07081.abstract: Multi-perspective-camera systems are widely adopted since they provide broad visual coverage for autonomous driving, motivating the synthesis of a unified wide view from spatially separated observations. In this work, we formulate wide view synthesis (WVS), which aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent wide view at a specified virtual viewpoint from multiple perspective cameras. Unlike conventional image stitching, WVS requires reasoning about 3D geometry and visibility to handle depth-dependent parallax and occlusions arising from spatially separated camera centers. While vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity view synthesis, its reliance on per-scene optimization limits its applicability to driving scenes. Furthermore, WVS introduces additional challenges, *e.g.*, peripheral stretching under perspective projection and photometric inconsistencies across cameras. To address these challenges, we propose **Wide-View Gaussian Splatting (WV-GS)**, a feed-forward Gaussian-splatting framework that synthesizes wide views without per-scene optimization. Specifically, we introduce Piecewise Perspective Rendering (PPR) to mitigate peripheral stretching through local perspective projections sharing a common camera center, and Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling (SAPM) to account for camera-dependent photometric variations during training. We further introduce **WideDrive**, a synthetic benchmark providing dense ground-truth wide views and adapt a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol to real-world datasets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS for WVS. Dataset and code will be publicly released.

papers.contribution: Proposes CoSafe, a cooperative runtime safety assurance framework using V2X communication for scene-level hazard monitoring and intervention in mixed-traffic autonomous driving.
papers.limitation: Evaluation is on simulation benchmark InterDrive; generalization to diverse real-world scenarios may be untested.
papers.gap: Integration of cooperative safety assurance with human driver behavior understanding and explainable intervention reasoning is not detailed.

papers.contribution: Introduces Jev-AD that combines a typed decision model with a language world model for foresight in highway merging, improving collision rates and aligning with passenger intent using predicted vehicle movements.
papers.limitation: Focuses primarily on highway merging scenarios; real-world deployment and scalability to broader conditions require exploration.
papers.gap: Extending language-model-backed foresight to multimodal contexts and explainable, human-centered driving assistance is unexplored.

papers.contribution: Analyzes training recipes for vision-language-action models in autonomous driving, revealing the impact of action-token supervision and gradient routing strategies on trajectory prediction and control performance.
papers.limitation: Study is on pretraining and training strategies; does not address downstream multimodal driving behavior interpretation or explanation.
papers.gap: Bridging training insights with explainable driving reasoning and multimodal human-centric interaction models remains open.

papers.contribution: Presents MotoVerse, a benchmark dataset for predictive perception focusing on motorized two-wheelers in dense, unstructured traffic with annotated challenges and multimodal data for anticipation and trajectory prediction.
papers.limitation: Zero-shot VLMs perform near simple baselines, indicating room for improved driving-specific multimodal understanding methods.
papers.gap: Integration of explainable reasoning and human-centered driver-state modeling for two-wheelers has yet to be addressed.

papers.contribution: Proposes a unified belief-space MPC that integrates information-seeking and risk-aware control adapting safety constraints dynamically as internal clarity about human intent evolves during interactive driving.
papers.limitation: Evaluations are limited to lane-merging and unsignalized intersection scenarios; broader traffic contexts and human behavior complexities remain untested.
papers.gap: Combining this risk-adaptive, interactive reasoning with multimodal sensory input fusion and explainable decision justification is a future direction.

papers.contribution: Develops Safety4DM, a vision-language system for vehicle-road-cloud cooperative dynamic maps, integrating a fine-tuned VLM for risk perception and a step-wise prompting interface for natural language querying and driving advice generation.
papers.limitation: System performance heavily depends on the quality of the fine-tuned VLM and simulation environment; real-world deployment constraints may pose challenges.
papers.gap: Further exploration is needed for multimodal fusion with onboard sensor data and personalized driver-state integration to enhance human-centered safety reasoning.

papers.contribution: Introduces DenseTwins, a self-supervised multimodal learning framework that decouples shared and modality-specific dense features, improving representation quality across multimodal perception tasks including autonomous driving.
papers.limitation: Focuses on representation learning benchmarks; direct applicability to downstream autonomous driving reasoning and explanations is not evaluated.
papers.gap: Extending learned dense features for explainable reasoning in driving behavior understanding is an open research avenue.

papers.contribution: Conducts a systematic study on transferability of pretrained backbones to multisensor autonomous driving setups, presenting targeted modifications improving MultiMAE for physical sensors fusion.
papers.limitation: Study centers on sensor backbone pretraining and transfer; connection to downstream driving behavior understanding and explanation remains indirect.
papers.gap: Bridging robust multisensor feature learning with interpretable multimodal driving reasoning models requires further work.

trends.finding: Emerging frameworks leverage multimodal fusion and language models to enhance driving behavior understanding and safety in autonomous and cooperative driving.
trends.uncertainty: Effectiveness varies across traffic complexities and real-world deployments; robustness and interpretability need more study.

trends.finding: Self-supervised and pretraining strategies improve multimodal feature representations but have limited direct impact on explainable driving reasoning or human-centered assistance.
trends.uncertainty: Connection between representation quality and downstream behavior understanding or explanation remains to be empirically validated.

trends.finding: Adaptive control integrating information-seeking with risk-aware planning enhances interaction modeling and safety in autonomous driving.
trends.uncertainty: Scalability to varied traffic scenarios and integration with multimodal perception data is not yet established.

comparisons.comparison: Cooperative runtime safety frameworks (CoSafe) use V2X for scene-level hazards versus individual agent foresight models (Jev-AD) focusing on ego-centric reasoning.
comparisons.limitation: CoSafe focuses on multi-agent interventions with limited language explainability; Jev-AD emphasizes foresight with language-based models but is mostly ego-centric.

comparisons.comparison: Vision-language-action model training methods differ on gradient routing and action-token supervision affecting control performance.
comparisons.limitation: Findings primarily relate to model training efficacy rather than human-centered explanation or interaction understanding.

comparisons.comparison: Benchmarks (MotoVerse, Safety4DM) target different traffic participants and contexts: two-wheelers in dense traffic versus cooperative vehicle-road-cloud safety contexts.
comparisons.limitation: Each dataset addresses specific challenges; integration for comprehensive multimodal driving behavior and explanation benchmarks is lacking.

ideas.question: Can cooperative runtime safety assurance be combined with language-based foresight models for explainable, multi-agent autonomous driving interventions?
ideas.hypothesis: Integrating V2X-based scene reasoning with language world models improves safety intervention explainability and effectiveness.
ideas.method: Combine CoSafe's V2X monitoring with Jev-AD's language-guided foresight; evaluate real-time intervention accuracy and explanation clarity.
ideas.metrics: Safety violations reduction, explanation fidelity, intervention success rate
ideas.compute: Real-time multi-agent simulation with V2X; moderate GPU for LLM inference
ideas.risk: Communication delays and model complexity may hinder real-time deployment.
ideas.novelty_check: No prior work combining cooperative runtime safety with language-driven foresight for explainable interventions.
ideas.priority_rationale: High significance for trustworthy, explainable mixed-traffic autonomous driving.

ideas.question: Does adding modality-specific dense representations improve multimodal driving behavior understanding and explainable reasoning models?
ideas.hypothesis: DenseTwins' decoupled dense features yield better multimodal fusion and enhanced explanation capabilities for driving behavior analysis.
ideas.method: Integrate DenseTwins pretrained embeddings into VLAs with evaluation on driving behavior prediction and explanation tasks.
ideas.metrics: Prediction accuracy, explanation quality, computation overhead
ideas.compute: Moderate GPU usage for dense embeddings and VLA inference
ideas.risk: Dense features may increase model complexity without clear explanation gains.
ideas.novelty_check: First application of decoupled dense features for explainable multimodal driving reasoning.
ideas.priority_rationale: Medium novelty, enabling better multimodal fusion for explanation.

ideas.question: Can clarity-aware, risk-adaptive MPC be extended to incorporate fine-grained multimodal perception and explainable decision outputs in interactive driving?
ideas.hypothesis: Integrating multimodal fusion into adaptive MPC enhances safety and interpretability in interaction-dense scenarios.
ideas.method: Augment the existing MPC framework with fused data inputs and add explainable risk attribution modules; benchmark on interactive driving simulations.
ideas.metrics: Success rate, collision rate, explanation coherence
ideas.compute: Moderate compute for MPC and multimodal fusion
ideas.novelty_check: Adaptive risk-aware MPC with integrated multimodal inputs and explanations is novel.
ideas.priority_rationale: High feasibility and significance for human-centered autonomous navigation.

papers.contribution: Introduces Traffic-VL, an 8B parameter vision-language model for direct multi-view image and natural language inputs to traffic signal control, trained via offline RL on photorealistic SynTra-V data, achieving robust generalization across topologies and conditions.
papers.limitation: Relies on simulation-to-real generalization; real-world deployment details are limited; model size and RL training complexity might constrain applicability.
papers.gap: Unclear how well the approach scales to highly dynamic or unstructured urban settings or integrates heterogeneous sensor modalities beyond cameras.

papers.contribution: Presents MultiMental-IAS, a large multimodal dataset for driver mental state analysis with synchronized EEG, PPG, vehicle telemetry, and video, enabling non-IID evaluation and driver-state personalization with detailed protocols.
papers.limitation: Data collected in a simulated driving cockpit may limit ecological validity; limited to 23 participants and certain induced states.
papers.gap: Application to real-world driving contexts with naturalistic stressors and broader populations remains to be explored.

papers.contribution: Proposes ReinSeg, a retrieval-guided multimodal framework combining LiDAR and surround-view images for accurate 3D road anomaly segmentation, improving detection and reducing false positives at high speed.
papers.limitation: Dependent on quality and alignment of camera-LiDAR data; reliance on frozen LIDO module may limit adaptability; tested on a specific benchmark (STU).
papers.gap: Integration with downstream autonomous driving planning and explanation modules not addressed; robustness in diverse weather or occlusion scenarios uncertain.

papers.contribution: Develops a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework for diffusion-driving vision-language-action models, dynamically adjusting inference depth and layer readouts, achieving speedup and improved trajectory error on Waymo E2E and nuScenes.
papers.limitation: Focuses on efficiency and per-scene adaptation without explicit interpretability of reasoning steps; tested on two datasets, generalization to other domains unclear.
papers.gap: Potential for incorporating explicit explainable reasoning mechanisms and human-understandable intermediate outputs.

papers.contribution: Presents STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy for vision-language action models in autonomous driving, enabling adaptive reasoning without manual scene-difficulty labels, optimizing route decisions for planning quality and inference efficiency.
papers.limitation: Evaluation limited to NAVSIM v1/v2; subjective complexity of driving scenarios might affect generalizability; implementation complexity of uncertainty-aware rollout.
papers.gap: Extension to real-world driving datasets and integration with multimodal perception inputs remains to be demonstrated.

trends.finding: Multimodal perception combining LiDAR, cameras, and driver state signals is increasingly leveraged to enhance autonomous driving behavior understanding and hazard detection.
trends.uncertainty: Effectiveness across varied real-world environments, sensor degradations, and cross-modal calibration remains partially untested.

trends.finding: Adaptive reasoning strategies in vision-language autonomous driving models are emerging to balance computational efficiency with planning performance, often via uncertainty-aware or scene-adaptive mechanisms.
trends.uncertainty: Impact on model interpretability and human-centered trust is not fully evaluated.

trends.finding: Vision-language multimodal models are applied beyond direct perception to operational levels such as traffic signal control, integrating RL and real-world evaluations, pointing to a shift towards end-to-end vision-language-based decision making.
trends.uncertainty: Scalability to complex, dynamic multi-agent urban settings and fusion with other sensor modalities are open challenges.

comparisons.comparison: Traffic-VL (2611.06353v1) directly learns control from images and language, achieving robust end-to-end traffic signal control, while ReinSeg (2611.02648v1) focuses on improving perception with multimodal retrieval for 3D anomaly segmentation.
comparisons.limitation: Traffic-VL mainly addresses decision making; ReinSeg focuses on perception enhancement. Integration of these modalities into a unified decision-making framework remains unexplored.

comparisons.comparison: STEER (2611.00718v1) and scene-adaptive readout (2611.02076v1) both address adaptive reasoning in autonomous driving VL models, but STEER explicitly avoids reliance on subjective scene-difficulty labels, whereas scene-adaptive readout leverages learned scene-conditioned weighting.
comparisons.limitation: Both methods are evaluated predominantly in simulation; real-world efficacy including interpretability and human trust aspects needs further investigation.

ideas.question: Can integrating multimodal driver state monitoring (EEG, PPG, telemetry) with LiDAR-image hazard detection improve prediction and explanation of risky driving behavior?
ideas.hypothesis: Fusing physiological and environmental signals enhances risk prediction accuracy and yields more grounded explanations of driver states.
ideas.method: Multimodal fusion networks with attention mechanisms; explanation modules linking driver state to perceived hazards.
ideas.baselines: Single-modality driver or hazard detection models
ideas.metrics: Macro-F1 for driver state, AP and FPR95 for anomaly detection, explanation faithfulness
ideas.compute: High, GPUs with fusion models; realistic latency targets
ideas.risk: Sensor synchronization challenges; overfitting to synthetic data
ideas.novelty_check: Combines driver internal states with external hazard perception multimodally; extends current separate modalities.
ideas.priority_rationale: High feasibility and significance for human-centered autonomous driving safety.

ideas.question: Does adaptive reasoning routing in driving VL models improve grounded explainability while reducing inference cost in real-world driving?
ideas.hypothesis: Adaptive routing that incorporates uncertainty-aware rollout can yield interpretable intermediate outputs with effective compute savings.
ideas.method: Extend STEER and scene-adaptive readout with human-understandable chain-of-thought explanations; evaluate on real driving datasets.
ideas.datasets: Waymo E2E, nuScenes, NAVSIM variations with added interpretation annotations
ideas.metrics: Planning accuracy, inference time, explanation quality assessed by human judges
ideas.compute: Moderate GPU usage; multiple seeds for stability
ideas.risk: Balancing explainability and efficiency may be conflicting; design complexity
ideas.novelty_check: Explicitly combines adaptive reasoning with explainable chain-of-thought in driving VL models.
ideas.priority_rationale: Important for trustworthy autonomous driving assistance and explanation.

ideas.question: Can vision-language reinforcement learning models trained on simulated photorealistic multi-view data generalize to diverse real-world urban traffic scenarios including complex driver interactions?
ideas.hypothesis: Augmented training on domain-diverse simulations improves RL policy robustness and multimodal perception generalization.
ideas.method: Train Traffic-VL-like models on expanded varied synthetic multi-view datasets; test on real-world varied topology scenarios with mixed traffic participants.
ideas.datasets: SynTra-V plus augmented urban simulations; real connected vehicle datasets
ideas.metrics: Traffic throughput, safety violations, generalization error
ideas.compute: Large-scale GPU clusters; long RL training
ideas.novelty_check: Extends vision-language RL to highly heterogeneous urban driving with richer multimodality.
ideas.priority_rationale: Addresses key gap in scaling to realistic urban driving complexity.

papers.contribution: Proposes an action-conditioned Vision-Language Model method to monitor autonomous vehicle behavior for semantic anomaly detection, combining video-based action prediction and ego-motion trajectory compatibility.
papers.limitation: Preliminary exploratory results on 235 clips; real-world generalization and response to diverse driving contexts remain uncertain.
papers.gap: Needs further validation on larger, diverse datasets and integration into real-time AV control systems for practical anomaly monitoring.

papers.contribution: Introduces VFlash, a fast, accurate visual planning method for predicting spatial primitives jointly to improve speed and accuracy in robot trajectory forecasting, enhancing planning success rates.
papers.limitation: Evaluated mainly on robot trajectory tasks; applicability and integration with autonomous driving multimodal data need further exploration.
papers.gap: Bridging VFlash's method to complex driving scenarios involving multimodal perception and planning is unexplored.

papers.contribution: Presents SM4RT, a cascade feed-forward model for unified 3D geometry reconstruction and motion estimation from RGB videos, improving dynamic scene reasoning for driving-related datasets.
papers.limitation: Depends on weakly supervised labels and benchmark datasets; robustness under real-world driving complexities not fully assessed.
papers.gap: Integration with multimodal data and real-time explainability for driving behavior understanding is not addressed.

papers.contribution: Offers a unified overview of safety certificate functions, synthesizing Hamilton–Jacobi reachability and control barrier functions for rigorous autonomous system safety reasoning and control synthesis.
papers.limitation: Focuses on theoretical and benchmark problems, but practical deployment challenges and integration with perception-driven explainable reasoning in driving remain open.
papers.gap: Applying these safety certificates to multimodal driving data and explainable anomaly detection is a frontier area.

papers.contribution: Develops an edge-assisted crowdsensing system with vision-language models and boosting machines for explainable cyclist safety perception using traffic attribute extraction and infrastructure data.
papers.limitation: Tested on limited UK routes; scalability and adaptation to diverse urban driving contexts with different sensors is uncertain.
papers.gap: Extending system for multimodal autonomous driving and integrating human-centered explanation mechanisms in driving behavior remains a gap.

papers.contribution: Argues for LLMs as supportive layers in underwater robotic missions for diagnostics and coordination under partial observability, distinguishing from direct control roles.
papers.limitation: Focuses on underwater robotics; transferring insights to autonomous driving contexts requires further investigation.
papers.gap: Opportunities to use LLMs for human-centered driver-state reasoning and explainable decision support in autonomous driving are suggested but undeveloped.

papers.contribution: Explores LLMs' ability to read and reason about neural network weights, finding capabilities limited to local arithmetic and memorization rather than true weight-flow tracing.
papers.limitation: Exploratory with single runs on small networks; generalization to larger systems and implications for explainable AI in driving remain tentative.
papers.gap: Implications for interpreting learned driving models and explainable reasoning in autonomous systems are not yet clear.

papers.contribution: Introduces UMBench, a fine-grained remote sensing benchmark for urban management tasks revealing current MLLMs' tendency to neglect fine-grained visual evidence and proposes evidence-first chain-of-thought method.
papers.limitation: Focused on urban remote sensing; direct applicability to vehicle driving scenarios and fine-grained driving behavior reasoning is indirect.
papers.gap: Advancing fine-grained visual reasoning and faithful explainability in complex driving environments remains underexplored.

trends.finding: Integration of multimodal perception (vision-language, 3D reconstruction) with task-specific reasoning (planning, anomaly detection) is critical for advanced autonomous driving behavior understanding.
trends.uncertainty: Real-world robustness and generalization of these methods beyond evaluated datasets are not fully validated.

trends.finding: Explainability and human-centered reasoning emerge as key focuses, particularly using structured models (EBMs) and evidence-prioritizing reasoning methods to provide transparent safety and behavior assessments.
trends.uncertainty: Scalability to diverse and real-time driving environments remains to be demonstrated effectively.

trends.finding: Large Language Models (LLMs) have potential roles as higher-level diagnostic and interaction layers supporting robotics and driving systems, though their direct reasoning about learned models or weights is currently limited and prone to memorization.
trends.uncertainty: The fidelity of LLM-based explanations and their integration into operational autonomous driving contexts require further research.

comparisons.comparison: VFlash and SM4RT both advance visual and geometric reasoning for planning and motion estimation but target different tasks and datasets; VFlash focuses on primitive decoding for trajectory planning, SM4RT on cascaded geometry and motion reconstruction.
comparisons.limitation: Neither explicitly incorporates multimodal data fusion with language or human-centered explanations.

comparisons.comparison: The edge-assisted crowdsensing system for cyclist safety (2611.08441v1) and the safety certificate overview (2611.07537v1) represent two complementary safety reasoning approaches: data-driven explainable prediction versus theoretical safety guarantees.
comparisons.limitation: They are not integrated, limiting joint verification of semantics and formal guarantees in autonomous driving monitoring.

comparisons.comparison: LLM studies (2611.07081v1, 2611.06162v1) highlight that while LLMs provide useful operational-level assistance, their capability for genuine reasoning about model internals or driving-specific learned representations is limited, contrasting with the more structured reasoning in EBMs or HJ/CBF safety certificates.
comparisons.limitation: Challenges remain to trust LLM-based reasoning for critical autonomous driving safety or explainability.

ideas.question: Can joint multimodal visual planning and trajectory reasoning improve anomalous driving behavior detection?
ideas.hypothesis: Combining VFlash-like visual primitive decoding with SM4RT's geometry-aware motion estimation improves anomaly detection in driving scenarios.
ideas.method: Integrated feed-forward visual planning and geometry-motion cascade model with anomaly scoring.
ideas.datasets: Use driving video datasets with anomaly labels and MolmoSpaces analogs (unverified).
ideas.baselines: Single modality motion estimation and visual-only anomaly detectors.
ideas.metrics: Anomaly detection accuracy, trajectory prediction error.
ideas.compute: GPU cluster, moderate memory, real-time feasible with optimization.
ideas.risk: Data complexity and integration challenges may limit performance gains.
ideas.novelty_check: Sample methods exist separately; joint approach novel.
ideas.priority_rationale: High potential to improve robust multimodal monitoring of driving behavior.

ideas.question: Does explicit incorporation of explainable safety certificates enhance trustworthiness and reliability of multimodal autonomous driving behavior monitors?
ideas.hypothesis: Integrating safety certificate methods (HJ reachability, CBFs) with interpretable visual-kinematic predictions yields better safety performance and explainability.
ideas.method: Fuse certificate-based control constraints with data-driven visual-kinematic inference models and explainable boosting machines.
ideas.datasets: Simulated vehicle systems and real-world driving scenarios (benchmark sets, unverified).
ideas.baselines: Purely data-driven anomaly detection and certificate-only control.
ideas.metrics: Safety violation rates, interpretability measures, task success rates.
ideas.compute: Moderate GPU/CPU resources; requirement varies by task complexity.
ideas.novelty_check: Existing isolated frameworks; combined application emergent.
ideas.priority_rationale: Bridges theory and practice, critical for deployable safe autonomous systems.

ideas.question: Can LLM-supported human-centered dashboard improve operator interaction and incident debugging for complex autonomous driving systems?
ideas.hypothesis: An LLM support layer anchored on multimodal sensor logs and system states enhances operator diagnosis and system orchestration, without replacing control.
ideas.method: Implement LLM-based natural language interaction module with structured state/log inputs for real-time assistance.
ideas.datasets: Driving system logs, telemetry, operator feedback datasets (unverified).
ideas.baselines: Standard operator tools and dashboards without LLM support.
ideas.metrics: Operator task time, error rates, user satisfaction.
ideas.compute: Server-grade compute for LLM inference with latency constraints.
ideas.risk: LLM errors and hallucinations may affect trust; failsafe required.
ideas.novelty_check: Inspired by underwater robotics use; novel in driving domain.
ideas.priority_rationale: Supports trustworthy and human-centered autonomous system use.

papers.contribution: Proposes a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for regulating profit-driven AMoD operators to limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability.
papers.limitation: Effectiveness limited during peak periods with high fleet utilization, and regulation depends on spare capacity and learned policies.
papers.gap: Unexplored integration with human-centered behavior modeling and multimodal traffic influences in regulatory dynamics.

papers.contribution: Reviews Max-Pressure traffic signal control algorithms, covering theory, extensions to multimodal/multiscale networks, CAV integration, and AI-enhanced methods.
papers.limitation: Theoretical foundations have remaining limitations; practical deployment challenges and integration with autonomous vehicle control need more study.
papers.gap: Underexplored coupling between explainable driving reasoning and AI-based Max-Pressure control in multimodal, automated environments.

papers.contribution: Presents integrated sensing and communication methods using cellular signals to detect and locate UAVs and road vehicles in complex environments with cooperative multi-site observations.
papers.limitation: Sensing affected by environmental complexities such as reflections and occlusions, and detection can suffer false positives requiring local checks.
papers.gap: Limited exploration of extracting explainable driving behavior or driver state from observed wireless sensing data in autonomous driving contexts.

papers.contribution: Investigates LLM capability to reason about neural network weights, concluding local arithmetic and dataset priors dominate over true weight-flow reasoning.
papers.limitation: Exploratory results from mostly single runs; verification of forward-pass tests lacking; generalization uncertain.
papers.gap: Application of such weight-space reasoning to interpret driving behavior models or explain autonomous driving reasoning remains unaddressed.

papers.contribution: Provides a closed-form analytical model explaining conditions under which home batteries create new local grid load peaks considering endogenous and exogenous prices.
papers.limitation: Model validated on a German case, uncertainty about generalizability; focus on grid load peaks rather than driving behavior or multimodal traffic interactions.
papers.gap: Does not address implications for multimodal autonomous driving or driver-state understanding in smart grid-integrated mobility.

trends.finding: Integration of AI and data-driven approaches is increasingly central to advanced traffic and mobility control methods.
trends.uncertainty: Extent to which these AI methods provide explainable, human-centered driving reasoning needs further validation.

trends.finding: Multimodal sensing and cooperation between sites enhance perception of complex driving and traffic scenarios using wireless signals.
trends.uncertainty: Robustness to environmental artifacts and mapping to driving behavior understanding is still limited.

comparisons.comparison: Multi-agent reinforcement learning regulation of AMoD (2611.07122v1) controls pricing and service, while Max-Pressure algorithms (2611.04029v1) focus on traffic signal optimization; both target improved traffic flow and service but via different control layers.
comparisons.limitation: Neither explicitly addresses transparent, explainable reasoning for autonomous vehicle behavior or driver state.

comparisons.comparison: Wireless ISAC sensing (2611.02157v1) offers detection data potentially useful for behavior analysis; LLM-based weight reasoning (2611.08070v1) explores understanding model internals but not linked to sensing data or driving reasoning.
comparisons.limitation: No direct combination of wireless sensing insights with learned weight and behavior explainability is demonstrated.

ideas.question: Can multi-agent RL-based AMoD regulation be enhanced with interpretable driver behavior models using wireless ISAC sensing?
ideas.hypothesis: Incorporating sensed driver state and behavior improves regulation policies and service equity.
ideas.method: Fuse ISAC data with multi-agent RL in simulation and real data; analyze policy interpretability.
ideas.datasets: Manhattan AMoD data plus ISAC sensing simulations.
ideas.baselines: Standard multi-agent RL regulation without integrated sensing.
ideas.metrics: Service availability, pricing fairness, interpretability scores.
ideas.compute: High for multi-agent RL with sensor fusion; GPU needed; multiple seeds.
ideas.risk: Data alignment challenges; sensing noise may degrade policies.
ideas.novelty_check: Combines regulation with ISAC sensing and interpretability rarely explored.
ideas.priority_rationale: High impact on human-centered AMoD regulation.

ideas.question: Can Max-Pressure signal control be integrated with autonomous vehicle onboard weight-space model reasoning to enable explainable driving decisions?
ideas.hypothesis: Coupling traffic signal control with vehicle-internal reasoning improves traffic flow and driving transparency.
ideas.method: Develop joint control-reasoning model combining MP algorithms and LLM-based weight interpreters.
ideas.datasets: Traffic network and simulated autonomous driving models.
ideas.baselines: MP control alone; LLM reasoning alone.
ideas.compute: Medium to high; simulations plus LLM inference.
ideas.novelty_check: Merges control theory with interpretable driving reasoning rarely combined.
ideas.priority_rationale: Bridges infrastructure and vehicle AI for autonomous driving explainability.

ideas.question: Does integrating economic grid load models with multimodal traffic control enable better autonomous driving behavior adaptation to local energy conditions?
ideas.hypothesis: Energy-aware behavior improves grid stability and driving efficiency.
ideas.method: Link home battery load peak models with driving route and signal control adjustments.
ideas.datasets: Grid load profiles; traffic data from reviewed papers.
ideas.metrics: Grid load peak reduction; travel time.
ideas.novelty_check: Novel crossover of grid load and autonomous driving control.
ideas.priority_rationale: Important for sustainable multimodal driving environments.
